Pretoria Eye Institute

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
...a private eye hospital is illegally fleecing patients and Medical Aid Schemes

Unique Selling Point:
A consumer story, relevant to all South Africans

Summary:
Jakes Scholtemeyer has been a Hospital Manager at the Life Hospital group for 21 years. He was headhunted by the Pretoria Eye Institute to become their CEO. It is privately owned by a group of 22 doctors. It was an eye opener, so to speak. He was confronted with a system designed to fleece the public and medical schemes as much as possible. There is also fraud and money laundering ongoing.

Further information:
Jakes Scholtemeyer, is the whistle-blower, CA & Hospital manager for 25 years, previous: Hospital Manager for Groenkloof Life Hospital. He was recruited by the Pretoria Eye Institute that also has day hospitals in Benoni and Fairie Glen
He soon found out that the hospital which is owned by 22 doctors has a sophisticated scheme going and is fleecing the patients and medical aid schemes in a major way. When he started to resist, he was first sidelined and then suspended, with all related Labour Court and CCMA issues. In January this year he made a protected disclosure to protect himself and filed a 195 page document. He has 8000 pages of documentation and can prove his allegations. There are also voice recordings.
The issues with the Institute are the following:

1. CONTRAVENING HPCSA REGULATIONS
• Incentivise doctors by:
o Setting targets
o Offering shares, shareholding determined by percentage over average
o Threaten to take privileges away: If targets are not met – forced to sell, get new one
• Diagnostic centre – proportional payments of dividends.
2. DEFRAUDING PATIENTS AND MEDICAL AID SCHEMES
• Phaco Cassettes -- Discovery forensics, Medscheme (Ophthalmology society), Gems, Polmed, Can cause loss of eyes, infections
• Unnecessary procedures
• Treat people at Day Hospital and charge acute fees
• Benoni never even had a practice number, operated for 12 years with no practice number, no anaesthesiology capability
• Faerie Glen has been on paper been owned by a fictitious company
• Consumables – cheat sheet

3. MONEY LAUNDERING AND FRAUD – PHARMACY
• Pharmacy set-up and control, Doctors cannot make money from pharmacies or dispensing
• No hospital may own a pharmacy
• Create their own pharmacy – appoint another owner that they can control
• Pharmacy is the only supplier to the hospital
• Pharmacy buys from a third company on the cheap, sell to hospital at inflated prices. Only supplier to PEI
• Third company owned by the doctors
• Jakes appointed director and owner of the pharmacy
• From Jan 2020 to June 2020 – accumulated R17 million in pharmacy account
• Problems:
o Ordered to transfer the shares to Francois Coopers family trust
o Liquidated the pharmacy
• Doctors withdrew the 17 million from the account.

4. OTHER ISSUES
• Optometrists on premises: Charge them exorbitant prices for rental of office space and charge them management fees as well as billing services.
• No financial statements for 14 years
• Owe SARS a possible R300 million
• No cash or stock control in the hospital

POTENTIAL INTERVIEWEES
• Jakes Scholtemeyer
• Francois Cooper
• Previous Pharmacy Manager
• Previous CEO of the Hospital
• Liquidator of the Pharmacy
• Hercules Hoffman (doctor)
• Pharmacy Council
• HPCSA
• Discovery
• Medscheme
• 2 patients who were treated at daycare and charge at acute hospital fees

Expert:
Prof. Alex van den Heever
Dr. Kgosi Letlape

Gauteng

Press Release:


Private Hospital Investigated

While private healthcare costs spiral ever higher, a hospital CEO from Pretoria made a protected disclosure alleging perverse incentives, over-servicing and recycling of single-use surgical items in a hospital owned by a group of doctors. Carte Blanche investigates what happened when the CEO accused his former employers of violating regulations of the Health Professions Council of South Africa (HPCSA) that prohibits doctors from participating in perverse incentive schemes as he was hauled before a disciplinary hearing. Is it a case of sour grapes from a disgruntled employee dismissed for serious improper conduct, or are the allegations of this former hospital CEO-turned-whistleblower being taken seriously?

Producer: Eugene Botha | Presenter: Claire Mawisa

Script:


V/O:
What would your reaction be when you are undergoing sensitive eye surgery and instead of using a new consumable device, your doctor re-uses a device that has been used hundreds of times before, although it is earmarked for single use only?

And, you discover that your doctor is being compelled to push through a minimum number of patients in order to fulfill aquota.
LINK:
These are exactly the allegations made by a whistle-blower in this 200-page document known as a Protected Disclosure. A protected disclosure is a document in which any employee may disclose information relating to an offence or a malpractice in the workplace by his or her employer or fellow employees.
V/O:
The Whistle-blower is Jakes Scholtemeyer and the document deals with alleged irregularities at the Pretoria Eye Institute in Arcadia, Pretoria. It is a private Ophthalmology Hospital owned by about 22 doctors who are also the shareholders. They are also involved in numerous companies relating to the hospital.

Scholtemeyer has been involved in private health care for decades, and was the Hospital Manager for the Life Groenkloof Hospital for 5 years, before he was invited to become the CEO of the Eye Institute on 1 April 2018.
LINK:
However, as time went by Scholtemeyer said he became increasingly uncomfortable with what he saw happening at the Institute.
Jakes:
For example, the board of directors, not all of them were registered per CIPC and formally appointed, that was a big concern to me. I was also surprised that various statements of various companies, were up to 11 years behind.
V/O:
He says his unease increased when shortly after his arrival, he was asked to sign a stack of letters to the doctors. He carefully read one of them.
Jakes:
And from the contents of this letter it was clear that the doctors were required to maintain a certain level of performance and admissions to retain their shareholding in the Pretoria Eye Institute.
LINK:
We also came in possession of the Memorandum of Incorporation of the Pretoria Eye Institute where it is clearly stated that shareholder, that is, the doctors of the Eye Institute is obliged to fulfill a certain quota of turnover for the hospital and if a doctor does not maintain this level of turnover, they are forced to sell their shares.
V/O:
Regulations published by the Health Professions Council prohibits physician incentives. In fact, they use the phrase “perverse incentives” to describe this.
Jakes:
Never ever are you allowed to entertain any scheme where doctors are directly or indirectly incentivized to admit patients at a hospital
V/O:
The reason for this is that incentives could cause overservicing and patients would be subjected to unnecessary procedures just to make up a quota.

When asked about this the Eye Institute, in a written answer, denied that they have a perverse incentive scheme and said that doctors are entitled to determine, as shareholders of a private company, that there should be a correlation between involvement with, or contribution to, the PEI by a doctor and shareholding.

Dr Kgosi Letlape a former President of the HPCSA condemns incentive schemes, and says the current healthcare regulations open loopholes for abuse.
Letlape:
If I am investor and I am a shareholder in a private clinic, I put my money there so that I can get a return on my money. I did not put my money there so that there should be better patient care. No. I am investor. On principle, I have refused to take shares from the private clinic I work in, because I don’t want to be conflicted.
V/O:
Scholtemeyer says, he also discovered that the Faerie Glen Eye Institute, a day facility, which is also owned by the doctors, had been operating for more than 10 years without having its own practice number. It was using the practice number of the Pretoria Eye Institute in Arcadia.
Jakes:
It is not allowed in the private healthcare industry that one facility is operated as an extension an extension of another facility, and each facility is required to have their own practice number.
V/O:
This is because different facilities have different fee structures. Fees at an acute hospital such as the Eye Institute are much higher than at a day hospital such as the Faerie Glen facility. Scholtemeyer says patients at the Faerie Glen day hospital could have been overcharged for a decade.

Professor Alex van den Heever is the Chair of Social Security Systems Administration and Management Studies at Wits, with expertise in Health Policy and Regulation.
Alex:
The use of another hospital’s practice number that had a different tariff structure that was higher than theirs would also be very problematic, illegal, because they are not charging for the services they are rendering. They are charging for the serices that can be rendered by the other facility.
V/O:
The Pretoria Eye Institute said regarding billing of patients at the day facility under the acute hospital tariff that

“This may have happened in a few cases in the past as an administrative issue. However, where such instances were picked up by the former CEO a few years ago, it was corrected.”

Scholtemeyer also discovered irregularities around consumable devices which, with accessories, cost around R3000 each. They are phaco casettes, and are used during cataract surgery.
LINK:
The Phaco Cassettes supplied to the Hospital were mainly single use items – where the manufacturer specified that the equipment can only be used once.
V/O:
However, Scholtemeyer says it was standard practice at the Eye Hospital to take the single-use cassettes, sterilize them and use them over and over again – up to 300 times. This is borne out by numerous documents in our possession.

We asked the Pretoria Eye Institute about this and they admitted re-use of single use items.

“Re-use of certain items is permitted, in instances where it meets the most stringent sterilization and safety requirements of the profession… This is strictly monitored and done with the knowledge of the suppliers.”

However, the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority or SAHPRA, in a communication to stakeholders, specifically on the topic of REPROCESSING OF SINGLE USE MEDICAL DEVICES, says it is not allowed:

“Reprocessing of any medical device which is intended by the original manufacturer for “single use” is in contravention of the Act.”
V/O:
Scholtemeyer says that when he started to phase out some of the irregularities, it had a massive impact on the Eye Institute’s earnings.
Jakes:
it affected the bottom line of the hospital substantially. We calculated at one stage that the bottom line nearly reduced by up to 50% due to the changes that were made.
V/O:
Scholtemeyer says he then started to experience negative sentiment towards him. Despite this, the doctors asked him to also take ownership of the pharmacy at the hospital. Between February 2020 and July 2020, the pharmacy accrued around eleven million rand in profit in its bank account.

Then one day, out of the blue, the Chairman of the Board informed him that they are relieving him, the CEO, of all financial duties.
Jakes:
I actually expected it, because I picked up that the doctors got concerned on the big profits in the pharmacy and it is actually in their mind in their minds, historically, their profits.
V/O:
But now Scholtemeyer was the owner of the pharmacy and says he was then put under severe pressure to relinquish ownership of the pharmacy. Because of this, he consulted a lawyer, who advised him to file a Protected Disclosure.

Acting on legal advice he also liquidated the pharmacy, with about forty-three million rand in the account, including the eleven million in profit.

Despite the pharmacy being under liquidation and the funds frozen, the Eye Institute withdrew all the money from the account. When asked about this the Eye Institute replied:

“Monies in the account of the HHSwart CC Pharmacy were used to pay creditors and employees in terms of the management agreement. The CEO and under his instructions, the financial managers of PEI had access as per the management agreement with the CC.”

However, documents in our possession seem to indicate that there was no management contract in place, and that there was even a discussion about how to directly access the profits of the pharmacy.

Scholtemeyer claims that this is a breach of Pharmacy Council and HPCSA regulations that prohibits prescribing doctors from benefiting directly from a pharmacy.

He goes on to say that he then reported the alleged irregularities to the HPCSA, Medical Aids, The Pharmacy Council, SAHPRA, and the Hawks.

From their side, the Pretoria Eye Institute informed us that Scholtemeyer is merely a disgruntled former employee, and that…

“during the second half of 2020 serious misconduct by him emerged and he was suspended. In February 2021 at last his hearing was conducted in the form of an arbitration. He was found guilty on all charges and dismissed by an independent arbitrator.”

Scholtemeyer has since instituted proceedings in the Labour Court against the Eye Institute.
LINK:
While our investigation has been focused on the Pretoria Eye Institute, we became aware of the fact that this actually a much bigger problem in private health care.
V/O:
Dr Letlape agrees and says that while unethical behaviour is to be condemned, one must also recognize that at the root, it is a systems problem.
Letlape:
It would not be correct to just look at a tip of the iceberg. Look at the system, look at how it is structured. You have corporatization of the systems where it is now run by corporates, and they make the rules. It is not run on professional behaviour, because you are now no longer treating the patient is a view of the best interest of the patient. You are treating a patient in accordance with the guidelines of the handlers of funds, the Medical Aids. You are not even being allowed professional autonomy.
V/O:
He says too much medical aid control and poor remuneration of doctors, linked to loopholes in regulation, create a fertile environment for unethical and unlawful behaviour in the sector.

Van den Heever agrees and says these issues were also identified in the Health Market Inquiry a few years ago.
Alex:
On the Health Market inquiry, if you look at the conclusions of that inquiry they said that medical scheme administrators effectively do not innovate to alter the structures that allow for the manipulation within the system. So, this is just one very crude example potentially, if the allegations are true, of what is in fact a systematic risk in the system.
V/O:
And Letlape says in the process the essence of healthcare is lost.
Letlape:
It is promotion of business and not promotion of ethical standards and professional behaviour. Because professionalism is not incentivized, so where do the incentives lie? In business practices that may be bordering on unethical or be plainly unethical. The greatest failure of regulators is not ensuring that the working environment of health care professionals is conducive to ethical behaviour.

LINK: While our investigation has been focused on the Pretoria Eye Institute, we became aware of the fact that this actually a much bigger problem in private health care. V/O: Dr Letlape agrees and says that while unethical behaviour is to be condemned, one must also recognize that at the root, it is a systems problem. Letlape: It would not be correct to just look at a tip of the iceberg. Look at the system, look at how it is structured. You have corporatization of the systems where it is now run by corporates, and they make the rules. It is not run on professional behaviour, because you are now no longer treating the patient is a view of the best interest of the patient. You are treating a patient in accordance with the guidelines of the handlers of funds, the Medical Aids. You are not even being allowed professional autonomy. V/O: He says too much medical aid control and poor remuneration of doctors, linked to loopholes in regulation, create a fertile environment for unethical and unlawful behaviour in the sector. Van den Heever agrees and says these issues were also identified in the Health Market Inquiry a few years ago. Alex: On the Health Market inquiry, if you look at the conclusions of that inquiry they said that medical scheme administrators effectively do not innovate to alter the structures that allow for the manipulation within the system. So, this is just one very crude example potentially, if the allegations are true, of what is in fact a systematic risk in the system. V/O: And Letlape says in the process the essence of healthcare is lost. Letlape: It is promotion of business and not promotion of ethical standards and professional behaviour. Because professionalism is not incentivized, so where do the incentives lie? In business practices that may be bordering on unethical or be plainly unethical. The greatest failure of regulators is not ensuring that the working environment of health care professionals is conducive to ethical behaviour.
